messages.content: You are the neutral rapporteur of a technology readiness review panel. Consolidate, attribute and preserve disagreement; do not decide and do not add technical claims of your own.

# Synthesis: assess · T03

## Claude Opus 5.5


# T03: MW-class waste-heat rejection (plant and tug)

## 0. Assumptions and split

**How T03 is split.** I rate four elements separately. Plant and tug differ by more than an order of magnitude in heat load and in heritage. The tug range of 50–800 kWth also mixes two different problems:

- **T03-P: plant heat rejection.** Rated per metallurgy route: P-NM (no-melt, carbonyl or H₂), P-RS (rotating smelter) and P-NA (narrow native-metal).
- **T03-T1: tug PPU and avionics pumped loop.** This loop removes about 4–6 % of electrical power, which is 50–150 kWth for a 1.0–2.5 MWe tug, at 320–370 K.
- **T03-T2: thruster self-radiation.** This is 25–40 % of electrical power, which is 250–1,000 kWth, radiated from the thruster bodies at roughly 500–800 K.

The 800 kWth upper bound only makes sense if it includes thruster losses. Those losses are radiated passively by the thrusters. They do not pass through a radiator loop, so they belong to the propulsion rating, not to T03 proper. **I recommend splitting T03 into T03-P and T03-T in the register.** The single YAML block at the end carries the plant, which is the governing, lowest-TRL element. The tug ratings are stated in the text and in the evidence entries.

**Radiator sizing.** Two-sided panel, ε = 0.85, effective sink 200 K. The panel must not view the sunlit NEA surface, which is 300–390 K at 1 AU. At 300 K that view would erase most of the net rejection.

| Radiator T | Net flux (two-sided) | Area for 1 MWth | Area for 9 MWth |
|---|---|---|---|
| 300 K | ~630 W/m² | ~1,600 m² | ~14,000 m² |
| 350 K | ~1,290 W/m² | ~770 m² | ~7,000 m² |
| 400 K | ~2,300 W/m² | ~430 m² | ~3,900 m² |
| 600 K | ~12,300 W/m² | ~80 m² | ~730 m² |

At an assumed 3–10 kg/m² for the radiator plus its share of loop and structure, a 9 MWth, 300 K plant radiator weighs 40–140 t. That mass feeds directly into D-02's economics gate. **The rejection temperature, which the route sets, matters more than the MW figure.**

**Plant heat cap (Claude's point).** Plant heat equals site electrical power (2.5–8 MW) plus any solar-thermal input to furnaces. A solar-thermal smelter could therefore exceed 9 MWth. The 9 MWth ceiling is valid only for all-electric routes. A sanity check supports the range: heating and melting 15–50 kt/yr of ore at about 1.5 MJ/kg gives 0.7–2.4 MW average for sensible and fusion heat alone, before losses.

**Other assumptions.**
- KDP-0B falls about 2032–2035. This is my assumption; no date is given.
- Plant life is 5–15 yr uncrewed with no EVA repair.
- Tug life covers multiple 1.5–5 yr round trips, about 10–15 yr in total.

## 1. Evidence

| # | Claim | Source | Scale and environment | Ratio to required | Confident |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| E1 | Pumped two-phase-free ammonia loops with deployable radiators reject heat in LEO for 20+ yr | ISS External ATCS, operational since about 2000–2002; design capacity about 70 kW across two loops | ~70 kWth, ~275 K coolant, crewed and maintained | Plant 14–130×; tug T1 0.7–2× | Yes for the ~70 kW design figure |
| E2 | Ammonia loops need EVA repair: pump-module failure and ammonia leaks | ISS pump module failure Dec 2010 (EVA replacement); P6 ammonia leak, EVA May 2013 | Same | n/a; shows uncrewed long-life leak isolation is *not* demonstrated | Yes |
| E3 | A rotating fluid joint carries ammonia between rotating radiators and the truss | ISS Thermal Radiator Rotary Joint (TRRJ) | ~35 kW per loop at ~1 rev/orbit (~0.001 rad/s) | P-RS: about 300× rotation rate (3 rpm), 10–100× heat | Yes for existence; rate approximate |
| E4 | Flight NaK radiator on a space reactor | SNAP-10A, 1965 | ~30–45 kWth, high-temperature conical radiator, ~43 days | 20–300× | Flight yes; thermal figure no |
| E5 | Flight NaK radiators on thermionic reactors | TOPAZ-I, Kosmos-1818 and -1867, 1987 | ~150 kWth class, high-temperature, months | 7–60× | Flights yes; kWth and radiator T no |
| E6 | Heat-pipe and loop-heat-pipe radiator panels in GEO, 15-yr uncrewed life | Commercial high-power GEO buses (generic heritage) | ~10–25 kWth per spacecraft, ~290–320 K | Plant 40–900×; tug T1 2–15× | Yes for the class; no single citation offered |
| E7 | Fission heat-transport and rejection chain run on the ground | KRUSTY / Kilopower, 2018, ground vacuum test | ~4–5 kWth reactor, ~1 kWe | 200–2,000× | Yes |
| E8 | MW-class space radiator design and component work | SP-100 (1983–1994); Prometheus/JIMO (2003–2005) radiator studies | Design studies plus component tests | Design studies are not TRL evidence | Programmes yes; specific radiator test data no |
| E9 | Ground water-heat-pipe radiator test for fission surface power | NASA GRC FSP technology demonstration work, ~2010–2014 | Single-digit to ~10 kWth class (believed) | ~100–1,000× | **No.** Verify before relying on it |
| E10 | Dust degrades radiators | Apollo LRV battery radiators fouled by dust; summarised in Gaier, "The Effects of Lunar Dust on EVA Systems During the Apollo Missions", NASA TM, 2005 | Lunar surface, small radiators | Qualitative only; NEA dust differs in charge and grain size, and gravity is ~10⁻⁴ g | Yes for Gaier 2005; TM number not quoted |
| E11 | Electrodynamic dust shield on a planetary surface | NASA KSC EDS on Firefly Blue Ghost M1, 2025 | Small coupons, lunar surface | Coupon-scale | **No.** I believe this flew and worked, but have not verified the details |
| E12 | 100-kW-class Hall thruster thermal steady state in vacuum | X3 nested Hall thruster at ~100 kW, NASA GRC, 2017 | Single thruster, chamber with cooled walls | T2: 10–25 thrusters per tug | Yes for test; thermal data publication not cited |
| E13 | Flight Hall-thruster self-radiation in deep space | Psyche, SPT-140 at ~4.5 kW, launched 2023 | ~1–1.5 kWth waste per thruster | 20–70× per thruster | Yes |
| E14 | Liquid-droplet radiator concept and drop-tower droplet tests | Mattick & Hertzberg concept (~1980s); Japanese microgravity droplet experiments | Concept and lab | Not credited above TRL 2–3 | Concept yes; experiment citations no |

Points to note:
- No MW-class radiator has flown, or been tested as a subsystem on the ground. The largest flown loop is about 70 kWth at about 275 K.
- No radiator has operated in an NEA proximity environment.
- No radiator has operated next to a self-generated dust and debris source. Tailings are 13–47 kt/yr.

## 2. Current TRL

| Element | Current TRL | Met at lower bound | Unmet for next level |
|---|---|---|---|
| **T03-T1** tug PPU loop, 50–150 kWth, 320–370 K | **5–6** | TRL 5: ISS and GEO hardware demonstrate components at this heat load and in vacuum (E1, E6) | TRL 6 or 7: no subsystem has been tested at tug specific-mass targets, in a 10–15 yr uncrewed, no-EVA, deep-space thermal environment. E2 shows the ISS loop relied on repair. |
| **T03-T2** thruster self-radiation, 25–40 kWth per thruster in clusters | **4–5** | TRL 4: lab thermal steady state at 100 kW (E12) | TRL 5: no validated thermal model of a multi-thruster cluster with mutual view factors and array back-loading. Chamber walls do not reproduce the deep-space sink. |
| **T03-P/P-NM** no-melt, mostly 300–400 K rejection, 3,900–14,000 m² for high loads | **3–4** | TRL 3: radiator physics and component behaviour validated (E1, E6) | TRL 4: no lab breadboard of a route-specific rejection chain with documented agreement to prediction. This includes microgravity condensing heat exchangers for H₂O from H₂-reduction off-gas, or for carbonyl condensers. The relevant environment (NEA dust, charging, IR view) has not been formally defined. |
| **T03-P/P-RS** rotating smelter, much heat rejectable at high T | **2–4** | TRL 2: concept documented. High-temperature radiators (E4, E5) and a rotating joint (E3) exist separately. | TRL 3 or 4: no test of a fluid rotary joint at 1–5 rpm and 10⁷–10⁸ rev, nor of co-rotating radiators at 0.05–0.15 g. No hot-slag or product direct-radiation heat-balance experiment. |
| **T03-P/P-NA** narrow native-metal, likely 1–3 MWth | **3–4** | Same as P-NM | Same as P-NM, at smaller scale |

**Plant overall: 3–4.** This is the governing element.

I do not credit modular scaling, meaning "a MW radiator is just N panels", above TRL 4. The panel-scale physics scales linearly. Deployment, structure, manifolding, leak and micrometeoroid isolation over 10⁴ m², and dust exposure do not.

## 3. Target and difficulty

**Targets.**
- **Plant: TRL 6 at KDP-0B, for the selected route only, with an internal 0A milestone of TRL 4–5 at the 0A mid-term review.**
  - Strictly, failure is an architecture change: the plant power is downsized. But heat-rejection mass and power cap throughput.
  - A plant that cannot reject 1–9 MWth at the route's temperature cannot pass D-02's economics gate.
  - So I treat it as project-ending for 0B, which under D-02 means no waiver.
  - Needed by about 2032–2035, my assumed KDP-0B date.
- **Tug T1: TRL 6 at KDP-0B** (AD² 3), because tugs deliver all 0B product.
- **Tug T2: TRL 6 at KDP-0B,** carried jointly with the EP thruster technology.

**AD² for the plant: 5, range 4–6.**
- The path is clear: modular heat-pipe or pumped panels, known coolants, existing large vacuum chambers.
- But nothing similar has been done at 10–100× scale, uncrewed for 10+ yr, beside a regolith-processing plant.
- By route:
  - P-NM and P-NA: AD² 5. The difficulty is low temperature, hence large area and mass, and condensing heat exchangers in microgravity.
  - P-RS: AD² 6. It depends on either a novel high-cycle rotary fluid joint or co-rotating radiators under spin load.
- Tug: T1 is AD² 3–4. T2 is AD² 4–5.

**Coolant and temperature by band.**

| Band | Coolant / transport | Leak isolation |
|---|---|---|
| 250–350 K | Ammonia pumped loop (ISS heritage) | Pumped loops need segmentation valves |
| 350–500 K | Water heat pipes, titanium or Monel, or an organic pumped loop | Heat pipes give per-pipe isolation (preferred for micrometeoroid and debris tolerance) |
| 500–800 K | NaK or Na/K heat pipes (SNAP and TOPAZ heritage) | Heat pipes give per-pipe isolation |

## 4. Path

| # | Step | Method | Scale | Cost (USD) | Duration | Reaches |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Route heat balance and temperature map. Define the relevant environment: NEA IR view, dust flux, charging, local debris from tailings, thermal cycling at 0.9–1.3 AU. | Analysis | All three routes plus tug | 0.3–1 M | 0.5–1 yr | Closes the TRL 4 environment-definition criterion |
| 2 | Coating and dust tests with CI/CM and ordinary-chondrite simulants. Vacuum, UV, electron flux; adhesion, α/ε change, EDS mitigation. | Experiment | Coupons, 0.01–0.1 m² | 2–6 M | 1.5–3 yr | Surfaces 4–5 |
| 3 | Panel breadboards at 300–400 K and 500–600 K in thermal vacuum. Include impact-puncture leak-isolation demo and a condensing-HX breadboard for the chosen route. | Experiment | 5–25 kWth panels | 5–15 M | 2–3 yr | 4–5 |
| 4 | Rotary fluid-joint life test (P-RS only). 1–5 rpm, ≥10⁷ rev accelerated, NaK or organic coolant. | Experiment | 50–500 kWth joint | 5–20 M | 2–4 yr | 4–5 |
| 5 | Subsystem segment: deployment plus thermal-vacuum performance. Gravity-offloaded deployment, in the NASA Armstrong Space Power Facility or equivalent. | Experiment | 200–500 kWth wing, 1/5–1/40 of plant | 40–120 M | 3–4 yr | 6 (segment) |
| 6 | Pathfinder flight panel at an NEA. Measure dust deposition and α/ε drift in situ. | Experiment (flight) | 5–50 kWth panel | 30–150 M incremental | 2–4 yr (rides on pathfinder) | 6–7 for panel and dust environment |
| 7 | Tug T1 subsystem: PPU cold plates, pumped loop and deployable radiator in thermal vacuum, plus a 10⁴-h life-test of pumps and valves. | Experiment | 100–150 kWth | 15–40 M | 2–3 yr | 6 |
| 8 | Tug T2 cluster thermal model validated against multi-thruster chamber data, with sink-temperature correction. | Simulation + experiment | 2–4 × 100-kW-class thrusters | 10–30 M (thermal increment) | 2–3 yr | 5–6 |

**Plant time to TRL 6: 6–10 yr.** Starting in 2027, this lands at 2033–2037. It is **at risk against a 2032–2035 KDP-0B**. Step 5 is the critical path and should start in 0A.

## 5. Risk and fallback

- **Plant:** project-ending for 0B through the economics gate. The technical failure mode is architecture change.
  - **Fallback:** cap plant thermal power at what a demonstrated segment design rejects within the mass budget.
  - Prefer routes and unit operations that reject heat at ≥500 K, or radiate hot slag and product directly.
  - If delivered $/kg then fails, fall back per D-02 to "0A only, Earth supply".
- **Tug T1:** schedule-delay or cost-increase. The fallback is ISS-derived heavier ammonia loops, at a specific-mass penalty.
- **Tug T2:** architecture change. The fallback is more thrusters at lower power each, or higher-efficiency thrusters to cut waste heat.

## 6. Where others might disagree

1. **Modular scaling.** Gemini or GPT may argue that MW plant radiators are "N × proven panels" and rate them 4–5. I hold 3–4 because deployment, manifold and leak-isolation behaviour over 10⁴ m², and dust next to the plant, are untested.
2. **ISS heritage for the tug.** One could rate T1 at 6–7 on ISS flight heritage. I cap it at 6 because ISS depended on EVA repair (E2), and the tug has a lower mass budget.
3. **Thermal ranking of routes.** Plausibly, the rotating smelter has the *easier* plant-level heat problem, since high-temperature rejection needs about 1/10–1/20 the area. Its rotary joint or spin structure is the harder part. The no-melt route has the hardest area and mass problem but no rotation. Which risk dominates is contestable.
4. **Risk class.** Calling the plant project-ending, rather than architecture-change, is a judgement that the economics gate binds. If Phase 1 demand tolerates a smaller plant, it reverts to architecture-change and a TRL 5 target.
5. **Unverified evidence.** E9 and E11 are unverified. The TOPAZ and SNAP-10A thermal figures are approximate.

## Gemini 3.1 Pro


### Evidence and Current TRL

The architecture requires two distinct waste-heat rejection systems: a 50–800 kWth system for the cargo tugs (operating in clean deep space) and a 1–9 MWth system for the processing plant (operating in a dusty, microgravity NEA environment). 

**1. Cargo Tug (50–800 kWth, clean vacuum):**
The International Space Station (ISS) External Active Thermal Control System (EATCS) utilizes pumped ammonia loops to reject approximately 70 kWth via deployable radiators at ~275 K. Scaling this to 800 kWth represents a 10× increase. Furthermore, to minimize radiator mass, high-power electric propulsion tugs typically require higher rejection temperatures (e.g., 350–500 K for Power Processing Units and thruster cooling), necessitating different coolants (such as water or organics like Dowtherm A) than the ISS ammonia system. While the basic principles of pumped fluid loops and heat pipes are TRL 9, autonomous leak isolation and scaling to 800 kWth at elevated temperatures are currently at **TRL 4–5**.

**2. Processing Plant (1–9 MWth, dusty microgravity):**
A 1–9 MWth rejection requirement is 15–130× larger than ISS capabilities. More critically, the plant radiators must operate in the immediate vicinity of active mining and beneficiation, exposing them to abrasive, charged regolith dust. Dust accumulation degrades radiator emissivity and can cause localized hot spots or mechanical jamming of deployment mechanisms. While passive and active dust mitigation technologies (e.g., electrodynamic dust shields) have been tested in laboratories (TRL 3–4) for solar panels and optical surfaces, they have not been integrated and validated on large-scale thermal radiators in a relevant environment. Consequently, the plant radiator system is at **TRL 3**.

**Current TRL Range:** 3–5. The lower bound (TRL 3) is met by analytical and experimental proof-of-concept for high-temperature coolants and preliminary dust mitigation. The unmet exit criterion for TRL 4 (for the plant) is component validation of dust-tolerant MW-class radiator segments in a laboratory environment.

### Target and Difficulty

**Target TRL:** 6 by KDP-0B (project-ending for Phase 0B, as the plant cannot operate without rejecting its waste heat).
**AD²:** 5 (New development; similar development has not been done at this scale and environment, but the path is clear through modular scaling and applied dust-shielding).

### Path to Target

1.  **Coolant & Materials Selection (Tug & Plant):** Analysis and subscale laboratory testing of high-temperature coolants (300–600 K) and compatible loop materials. (Reaches TRL 4).
2.  **Dust Mitigation Breadboard (Plant):** Vacuum-chamber testing of radiator surface coatings and active dust-shedding mechanisms (e.g., EDS) under simulated charged NEA dust bombardment. (Reaches TRL 4/5).
3.  **Subscale Modular Prototype (Tug & Plant):** Thermal-vacuum testing of a ~50–100 kWth modular radiator wing, demonstrating automated deployment, fluid loop stability, and leak isolation valves. (Reaches TRL 5).
4.  **Integrated System Prototype (Plant):** Thermal-vacuum testing of a multi-module array with integrated dust mitigation and simulated thermal loads. (Reaches TRL 6).

### Risk and Fallback

**Risk if fail:** Project-ending (for 0B). Without MW-class heat rejection, the processing plant will rapidly overheat, rendering in-space production impossible.
**Fallback:** Drastically reduce plant throughput to lower thermal loads, or revert to "0A only, Earth supply".

### Where others might disagree

Others might argue that because radiators are highly modular, flying a 70 kWth system on ISS means a 7 MWth system is just 100 copies of the same thing, implying a higher TRL. However, this ignores the non-linear complexities of manifolding, pumping massive fluid volumes, autonomous leak detection/isolation across a massive area, and the severe operational hazard of electrostatic dust coating the thermal surfaces.

## GPT-6.1 Sol


## T03 — MW-class waste-heat rejection

**Assessment:** Established spacecraft thermal-control technologies support development, but they do **not** establish readiness of a multi-megawatt, dust-exposed NEA plant or a megawatt-electric cargo tug.

| Application | Current TRL | Target at KDP-0B | AD² | Principal qualification gap |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Plant, stationary no-melt process | **3–4** | **6** | **5** | MW-scale integration, dust, thermal cycling and fault isolation |
| Plant, rotating smelting process | **2–3** for the rotation-dependent heat-transfer subsystem | **6** | **6** | Heat transfer across or within rotating equipment; process/radiator temperature separation |
| Plant, narrow native-metal route | **3–4** if stationary; **2–3** if rotation-dependent | **6** | **5–6** | Depends on the experimentally selected process |
| Tug, integrated thermal management | **3–4** | **6** | **5** | PPU/thruster heat partition, deployed radiator scale, lifetime and propulsion integration |

These are ratings of **T03 at the required scale and environment**, not ratings of ammonia loops, heat pipes or radiators considered individually. The higher bounds are conditional on obtaining applicable breadboard test reports; they are not established by the architecture description alone.

### Assumptions and thermal definition

- **Plant:** 1–9 MWth is an assessment envelope, not an independently validated heat load. Each route must close an energy balance. Heat rejected cannot exceed electrical power dissipated on site **plus explicitly stated absorbed solar-thermal and other thermal inputs**, less energy leaving through products, exhaust or other pathways. The 9 MWth case therefore needs justification against the 2.5–8 MWe site supply.
- **Plant duration:** not specified. I provisionally assume a **five-year operating campaign**, with replaceable radiator modules. A different requirement changes lifetime qualification.
- **Tug:** 50–800 kWth must be separated into **PPU/electronics cooling**, **thruster structural heat rejected by self-radiation**, and any other spacecraft cooling loads. Energy carried away in the exhaust is not a radiator load.
- **Tug duration:** 20,000–40,000 propulsion operating hours, with 1.5–5-year round trips. Those hours do not establish the complete calendar-life requirement.
- **Environment:** vacuum, microgravity or rotating 0.05–0.15 g hardware, 0.9–1.3 AU illumination and thermal cycling, radiation, and—in the plant’s case—abrasive charged regolith and deposition. Tug dust exposure depends on docking and loading operations.

**Temperature and coolant must remain route-specific:**

| Circuit | Assessment reference | Candidate coolant; limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Plant low-temperature auxiliaries | Radiating surface approximately **300–350 K** | Water or ammonia-based architecture; freezing, containment and materials compatibility require qualification |
| Plant process heat rejection | Approximately **450–600 K**, **only where the process permits** | Pressurised water at suitable temperatures, or qualified liquid-metal/heat-pipe circuits; no coolant selection is established |
| Tug PPU/electronics | Approximately **300–350 K** initially | Water/ammonia or another qualified fluid; actual set point follows electronics limits and thermal resistance |
| Tug thruster structure | Temperature set by selected thruster | Predominantly direct radiation where demonstrated by the thruster design; not automatically a shared pumped loop |

Ammonia is **not** a generic coolant across the entire 300–600 K range. Equally, a hot furnace does not justify assuming that all plant auxiliary heat can be rejected at 600 K.

For scale, using emissivity 0.9 and neglecting absorbed sunlight and mutual irradiation:

\[
A_{\rm emitting}=\frac{Q}{0.9\,\sigma T^4}
\]

- Plant at **300 K:** approximately **2,400–21,800 m²** emitting area.
- Plant at **600 K:** approximately **150–1,360 m²**.
- Tug at **300 K:** approximately **120–1,940 m²**.
- Tug at **350 K:** approximately **65–1,050 m²**.

These are **total emitting areas**, not necessarily deployed planform areas. They are optimistic screening values, not qualified designs. Solar flux is approximately **805–1,680 W/m²** over 1.3–0.9 AU; shielding, orientation, dust-induced absorptivity changes and view factors can materially increase required area.

## 1. Evidence

### ISS external active thermal control

**Sources:** NASA, *Reference Guide to the International Space Station* (2015); NASA’s documented Expedition 24 external ammonia pump-module replacement operations, August 2010.

- **Demonstrated:** operational pumped-ammonia heat transport, external radiators, control and maintainable hardware in orbital vacuum and microgravity.
- **Scale:** two external loops, each with a published **approximately 35 kW heat-rejection capacity**.
- **Important qualification:** 35 kW is a published capacity, not a calorimetrically verified full-load operating result established by the sources cited here. I do not equate installed capacity with demonstrated maximum sustained rejection.
- **Required/rated scale ratio:**
  - Plant versus the approximately 70 kW two-loop system: **14–129×**.
  - Tug versus one approximately 35 kW loop: **1.4–23×**.
- **Mismatch:** relatively low-temperature operation; Earth-orbit rather than NEA illumination; no asteroid regolith environment; servicing history does not demonstrate autonomous leak recovery.

**What it supports:** mature underlying low-temperature thermal-control functions. It does not qualify a scaled NEA implementation.

### SNAP-10A

**Source:** US SNAP-10A flight programme, launched in **1965**.

- **Demonstrated:** an approximately **30 kWth** reactor with liquid-metal heat transport and space heat rejection; approximately **500 We** output; roughly **43 days** of operation in orbit.
- **Scale:** heat rejected was approximately **30 kW**, allowing for the small electrical output.
- **Required/demonstrated scale ratio:**
  - Plant: approximately **33–300×**.
  - Tug total heat-load envelope: approximately **1.7–27×**.
- **Mismatch:** a hotter reactor/converter architecture, not a matched 300–600 K NEA process radiator; no dusty operating site; duration far below the required multi-year service.
- **Uncertainty:** I am not assigning a specific demonstrated radiator surface temperature here without the original thermal-performance report.

**What it supports:** liquid-metal heat transport and space radiation are physically demonstrated, not speculative. It does not establish the proposed module size, deployment, contamination tolerance or lifetime.

### Evidence limitation

I cannot confidently identify, from the evidence available here, a physical demonstration combining:

> **MW-class rejection + the selected coolant and radiator temperature + NEA dust + representative deployment + autonomous isolation + required lifetime.**

I therefore give **no TRL uplift** for Project Dyson design studies, panel agreement or unverified radiator proposals.

## 2. Current TRL and unmet exits

### Stationary plant: TRL 3–4

- **Lower bound, TRL 3:** spacecraft heritage experimentally validates the critical functions of pumped heat transport and radiative rejection.
- **Conditional upper bound, TRL 4:** defensible for a defined implementation built around tested components, provided documented laboratory breadboard results agree with predictions and define the relevant environment.
- **Next unmet exit, TRL 5:** documented breadboard performance in the **relevant environment**, with explicit scaling requirements. The missing combination includes representative temperature, coolant, dust deposition, solar loading and isolation behaviour.

The upper bound is **not** a claim that the full plant has already passed laboratory validation.

### Rotating-smelting plant: TRL 2–3

There are two materially different architectures:

1. **Stationary radiator connected across a rotating interface:** rotary fluid joints, seals, hoses or other transfer hardware become a critical subsystem.
2. **Radiator and loop rotate with the furnace/module:** avoids that interface but introduces rotating deployment, fluid behaviour, structural loading and view-factor constraints.

- **TRL 2 is supported:** a documented application can be formulated from established principles.
- **TRL 3 is conditional:** it requires an applicable experiment validating the selected rotation-dependent critical function. None is identified here.
- **Next unmet exit from the lower bound:** experimental or test-validated analytical proof of that critical function.

This rating concerns **heat rejection associated with the route**, not the metallurgical readiness of the furnace.

### Narrow native-metal production

- **Stationary processing:** **TRL 3–4**, as above.
- **Rotating modules:** **TRL 2–3** for the rotation-dependent subsystem until physically demonstrated.

“Experimentally gated” is an appropriate programme posture, but is not TRL evidence.

### Tug: TRL 3–4

- Existing thermal-control heritage supports the critical physics.
- The integrated tug rating remains limited by the unspecified thruster, propellant, PPU efficiency, heat partition, radiator design and duty profile.
- **Next unmet exit, TRL 5:** a representative PPU/thruster thermal breadboard operating in vacuum with the selected heat-load partition, radiator temperature, scaling definition and fault response.

Thruster self-radiation cannot be credited at the required scale merely because smaller electric thrusters operate in space.

## 3. Target and difficulty

**D-02 target:** **TRL 6 at KDP-0B**, with no waiver for the architecture-critical thermal system.

**Needed by:** KDP-0B, **before commitment to production hardware and cargo-tug procurement**. No calendar date for that milestone is supplied.

**Internal 0A milestones:** TRL **4–5**, using ground breadboards and a pathfinder where useful.

| Application | AD² to TRL 6 | Reason |
|---|---:|---|
| Stationary plant | **5** | Clear physical path, but the combined scale/environment demonstration is not established |
| Rotation-dependent plant | **6** | Competing configurations; thermal interfaces and rotating radiator architecture remain unresolved |
| Tug | **5** | Established technology families, but substantial propulsion-specific integration and lifetime development |

These use the project’s AD² anchors. Their nominal percentages should **not** be interpreted as independently derived project success probabilities.

**Indicative time:** **4–8 years** to relevant-environment TRL 6 for stationary plant/tug hardware, assuming early interface selection and parallel facilities work. A rotation-dependent route or mandatory flight precursor could extend this to **5–10 years**.

## 4. Path to qualification

Costs below are **rough-order engineering estimates in 2026 USD**, not quotations. They exclude the production fleet and major launch services unless explicitly included.

| Step | Test or analysis | Scale and environment | Cost | Duration | Exit supported |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| Close heat budgets and heritage evidence | Analysis plus literature audit | Every process route; 1–9 MW plant and 50–800 kW tug envelopes | **$0.5–2M** | **0.5–1 yr** | Defines application and scaling; **does not alone raise TRL** |
| Critical-function breadboards | Experiment | **10–50 kW** vacuum loops; coatings, dust coupons, thermal cycling, valves, puncture/isolation tests; rotating interface if selected | **$5–15M** | **1–2 yr** | **TRL 3–4** |
| Relevant-environment module | Experiment with correlated model | **100–300 kW** module; actual coolant and temperature; solar simulation, charged-dust exposure and repeated fault isolation | **$15–45M** | **1.5–3 yr** | **TRL 5** |
| Plant subsystem demonstration | Experiment | At least **1 MW aggregate**, with representative module/manifold topology, controls, deployment and process-load transients | **$40–120M** | **2–4 yr** | **TRL 6**, only if scaling to selected maximum load is validated |
| Tug propulsion/thermal demonstration | Experiment | Selected propulsion configuration at **1–2.5 MWe**, including PPU loop and measured thruster self-radiation; up to the selected **800 kWth** thermal case | **$30–100M** | **2–4 yr** | **TRL 6** |
| Optional flight precursor | Experiment | **50–150 kW** deployable module at representative solar loading; autonomous isolation and thermal cycling | **$80–250M** | **3–5 yr** | **TRL 7 for that prototype**, not automatically the MW system |

The plant and tug demonstrations may share component development, but **neither substitutes for the other**.

### Required qualification details

- **Dust:** measure changes in solar absorptivity and infrared emissivity against deposited mass and particle distribution. Demonstrate shielding or cleaning without unacceptable plume, abrasion or contamination effects.
- **Leak isolation:** segmented inventory, independently isolatable modules, inventory-loss detection and surviving-capacity tests. Demonstrate a puncture or induced leak rather than relying only on valve-command simulations.
- **Lifetime:** endurance testing and a test-correlated degradation model covering pumps, seals, heat pipes, coatings, radiation and start/stop cycles. A short vacuum test does not establish 20,000–40,000 hours.
- **Gravity:** ground tests alone may not bound two-phase fluid distribution or rotating interfaces. Use relevant-gravity testing or flight evidence where the governing behaviour cannot be adequately reproduced.
- **Scale:** a 1 MW test does not automatically qualify 9 MW. Modular extrapolation must validate common manifolds, hydraulic stability, controls, deployment and correlated failures. Otherwise increase test scale or narrow the operating envelope.

## 5. Risk and fallback

**Primary risk class: project-ending for 0B** if neither a stationary plant nor the required tug fleet can meet heat-rejection requirements. D-02 then implies **0A only, Earth supply**.

More local failures have different consequences:

- **Rotating thermal interface fails:** **architecture-change**—use stationary no-melt/native-metal processing if independently qualified.
- **High-temperature loop fails:** **architecture-change/cost-increase**—use lower-temperature, larger radiators if mass, deployment and power budgets close.
- **Tug thermal envelope fails:** **architecture-change**—reduce propulsion power, use more vehicles or lengthen transfer schedules, subject to demand and economics gates.
- **Qualification overruns:** **schedule-delay**, not justification for a TRL waiver.

Radiator redundancy is not a substitute for qualifying common-mode dust deposition, coolant loss or deployment failure.

## 6. Where others might disagree

1. **TRL 3 versus 4:** component specialists may credit mature loop hardware as TRL 4 or higher. That is reasonable for the component, but not automatically for the integrated architecture. The upper bound requires applicable test documentation.
2. **Whether MW operation is essential for TRL 6:** validated modular scaling may justify a smaller prototype. I would accept that only after demonstrating representative shared interfaces and bounding the maximum-load failure modes.
3. **Rotation-dependent rating:** an existing tested rotary thermal interface could raise it. None has been identified here at the required coolant, temperature, environment and lifetime.
4. **Tug heat partition:** a well-qualified, predominantly self-radiating thruster could substantially reduce radiator requirements. Conversely, assigning the entire 800 kWth to a low-temperature PPU loop makes the tug much harder.
5. **Dust severity:** shielded radiator placement may reduce exposure dramatically. That is an experimentally testable architectural benefit, not grounds to omit contamination qualification.

# T03 consolidated rating: MW-class waste-heat rejection (plant and tug)

This is the rapporteur's consolidation of three assessments: Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-6.1 Sol. It attributes each position and preserves disagreements. The panel decides.

## 1. Ratings by model

### 1a. Headline (YAML) values

| | Claude Opus 5.5 | Gemini 3.1 Pro | GPT-6.1 Sol |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scope of YAML block | Plant only (the governing element). Tug rated in text. | Plant and tug combined | Plant and tug combined |
| Current TRL | 3–4 | 3–5 | 2–4 |
| AD² | 5 | 5 | 6 |
| Target | TRL 6 at KDP-0B. Internal TRL 4–5 at 0A mid-term. | TRL 6 at KDP-0B | TRL 6 at KDP-0B, no waiver. Internal 0A milestones TRL 4–5. |
| Risk class | Project-ending (0B) | Project-ending (0B) | Project-ending (0B) |
| Years to target | 6–10 | 3–5 | 4–10 |
| Confidence | medium | medium | medium |

### 1b. Per-element breakdown in the text

| Element | Claude | Gemini | GPT |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plant, stationary no-melt | TRL 3–4; AD² 5 | TRL 3 (plant, not split by route); AD² 5 | TRL 3–4, upper bound conditional; AD² 5 |
| Plant, rotating smelter | TRL 2–4; AD² 6 | Not addressed | TRL 2–3 for the rotation-dependent subsystem; AD² 6 |
| Plant, narrow native-metal | TRL 3–4; AD² 5 | Not addressed | TRL 3–4 if stationary, 2–3 if rotating; AD² 5–6 |
| Tug PPU/avionics loop | **T1: TRL 5–6**; AD² 3–4 (50–150 kWth, 320–370 K) | Tug as one element, **TRL 4–5** (50–800 kWth at 350–500 K) | Integrated tug **TRL 3–4**; AD² 5 |
| Tug thruster self-radiation | **T2: TRL 4–5**; AD² 4–5. Carried jointly with EP. | Folded into the single tug rating | Folded into the integrated tug rating. Not credited from small-thruster heritage. |

### 1c. Years and risk detail

**Years to target:**
- Claude: 6–10 yr for the plant. From a 2027 start this gives 2033–2037. Claude rates this "at risk" against an assumed 2032–2035 KDP-0B.
- GPT: 4–8 yr for stationary plant and tug. 5–10 yr if the route is rotation-dependent or a flight precursor is mandatory.
- Gemini: 3–5 yr, with no breakdown.

**Risk-class sub-cases:**
- Claude:
  - The plant rating of project-ending is "a judgement that the economics gate binds". It reverts to architecture-change, with a TRL 5 target, if Phase 1 demand tolerates a smaller plant.
  - T1 is schedule-delay or cost-increase.
  - T2 is architecture-change.
- GPT:
  - Failure of the rotating interface is architecture-change.
  - Failure of the high-temperature loop is architecture-change or cost-increase.
  - Failure of the tug thermal envelope is architecture-change.
  - Qualification overruns are schedule-delay, and do not justify a waiver.
- Gemini gives no sub-cases.

## 2. Where the models agree

- **No MW-class demonstration exists.** All three cite the ISS External ATCS (about 70 kWth total) as the largest relevant flight heritage. They give similar plant scale ratios: 14–130× (Claude), up to 130× (Gemini) and 14–129× (GPT). No model identifies a MW-class radiator that has flown or been ground-tested as a subsystem.
- **Modular scaling earns no extra credit.** All three explicitly reject "MW radiator = N × proven panels" as grounds for a higher TRL. They cite four untested behaviours:
  - manifolding;
  - deployment;
  - autonomous leak and micrometeoroid isolation over large areas;
  - common-mode dust exposure.
- **Dust is unqualified.** All three treat dust degradation of α/ε near an active regolith-processing plant as untested, and require dust and coating testing on the path.
- **Autonomous leak isolation is undemonstrated.** Claude and GPT both note that ISS ammonia-loop operations depended on crew/EVA servicing. Gemini lists autonomous leak isolation as an open gap.
- **Target and consequence.** All three set TRL 6 at KDP-0B and classify failure as project-ending for 0B. The ultimate fallback in each is "0A only, Earth supply" per D-02.
- **Rejection temperature drives area.** Claude and GPT both stress that the route-dependent rejection temperature matters more than the MW figure. Gemini also cites a 300–600 K range.
- **Rotating route.** Claude and GPT agree that rotation-dependent heat rejection is the lowest-TRL plant case, with AD² 6. Gemini does not address it.
- **Internal milestone.** Claude and GPT both set an internal milestone of TRL 4–5 within 0A.

## 3. Where the models diverge, and what would settle it

### D1. Tug scope and rating: 3–4 vs 4–5 vs 5–6

This is the largest numerical divergence. It stems mainly from how each model defines the tug heat load.

- **Claude:**
  - Argues the 800 kWth upper bound is meaningful only if it includes thruster losses.
  - Says those losses radiate passively from the thruster bodies at about 500–800 K and belong with propulsion.
  - Leaves the radiator loop (T1) with 50–150 kWth, which is 0.7–2× ISS.
  - On that basis rates T1 at 5–6.
  - Evidence relied on: ISS EATCS (E1), generic GEO heat-pipe bus heritage (E6, no specific citation), X3 at about 100 kW (E12) and Psyche SPT-140 (E13).
- **Gemini:**
  - Treats the full 50–800 kWth as a radiator-system load, which is about 10× ISS, at 350–500 K.
  - Rates it 4–5 on ISS heritage plus the change of coolant.
- **GPT:**
  - Says the PPU/thruster partition is unspecified and must be defined before rating.
  - Rates the integrated tug 3–4.
  - Declines to credit thruster self-radiation from the operation of smaller thrusters in space.
  - Notes the partition cuts both ways: a well-qualified self-radiating thruster could substantially reduce the radiator load; assigning all 800 kWth to a low-temperature PPU loop makes the tug much harder.

**What would settle it:**
1. A defined heat partition for the selected thruster and PPU. All three models flag this, and Claude's and GPT's path step 1 includes it.
2. Measured partition data from a tug propulsion/thermal test: Claude steps 7–8, or GPT's integrated tug demonstration.
3. The X3 thermal-data publication, which Claude says it has not cited.

A separate panel question is whether T03 should be split into a plant item and a tug item in the register (see D7).

### D2. Plant upper bound: TRL 3 vs 4

- **Gemini** rates the plant at TRL 3. Its reason is that dust mitigation has not been integrated on radiators.
- **Claude** rates 3–4.
- **GPT** also rates 3–4, but states that TRL 4 is conditional on obtaining applicable breadboard test reports. GPT says the architecture description does not establish it.

**What would settle it:** a documented lab breadboard of the route-specific rejection chain, with results agreeing with prediction. This means panels plus condensing heat exchanger, or a rotary joint for the rotating smelter. It also needs a documented definition of the NEA relevant environment.

Claude and GPT phrase the unmet criterion in essentially these terms. Gemini's phrasing is "component validation of dust-tolerant MW-class radiator segments in a laboratory environment".

### D3. Rotating-smelter bound: 2–4 vs 2–3

- **Claude** allows an upper bound of 4. It cites a high-temperature NaK radiator (E4, E5) and the ISS Thermal Radiator Rotary Joint (E3) as existing separately.
- **Claude also argues** that the rotating smelter may have the easier plant-level heat problem, because high-temperature rejection needs about 1/10–1/20 the area. On this view its rotary joint or spin structure is the harder part.
- **GPT** caps the rotating case at 3. It also cautions that "a hot furnace does not justify assuming that all plant auxiliary heat can be rejected at 600 K."
- **Gemini** is silent on this route.

**What would settle it:** either of the following.
- A rotary fluid-joint life test at 1–5 rpm and at least 10⁷ revolutions (Claude step 4).
- A located test record of an existing rotary thermal interface at the required coolant, temperature, environment and life (GPT).

Separately, a route heat-balance map would show what fraction of route heat can actually be rejected at high temperature.

### D4. Years to TRL 6: 3–5 vs 4–10 vs 6–10

The spread follows from what each model treats as sufficient for TRL 6.

| Model | Test article treated as sufficient for TRL 6 | Flight element |
|---|---|---|
| Gemini | 100–250 kWth array in dusty thermal-vacuum testing | None |
| Claude | 200–500 kWth wing in a large chamber (1/5–1/40 of plant) | Plus an NEA pathfinder flight panel to characterise dust and α/ε drift in situ |
| GPT | At least 1 MW aggregate, unless validated modular scaling of shared interfaces is shown | Optional precursor, which extends the range |

**What would settle it:** the panel defining the minimum TRL 6 test scale and whether NEA in-situ dust data is required. This is a criterion decision rather than an evidence question. The KDP-0B calendar date also matters: Claude assumes 2032–2035; GPT and Gemini give no date.

### D5. AD² for the combined item: 5 vs 6

- **Claude** gives 5 for the plant, with range 4–6.
- **Gemini** gives 5.
- **GPT** gives 6 in its YAML.

At element level the three are close: Claude and GPT both give 5 to the stationary plant and 6 to the rotating route. The YAML difference reflects that GPT's single block takes the rotation-dependent case as headline, while Claude's takes the plant as a whole.

**What would settle it:** a route selection, or a decision on the register split (see D7).

### D6. Duration requirement

The models use different service-life assumptions. None was supplied as a requirement.

| Model | Plant | Tug |
|---|---|---|
| Claude | 5–15 yr uncrewed, no EVA | About 10–15 yr total |
| Gemini | Multi-year | 1.5–5 yr |
| GPT | Provisional 5-yr campaign, replaceable modules | 20,000–40,000 propulsion hours. GPT notes these hours do not set calendar life. |

**What would settle it:** a requirement from the architecture owner. Lifetime qualification scope depends on it.

### D7. Register structure

- **Claude** recommends splitting T03 into T03-P (plant) and T03-T (tug).
- **GPT** rates the applications separately but keeps one YAML block.
- **Gemini** keeps a single item.

This is a panel decision.

### D8. Heat-load ceiling and radiator area

**The 9 MWth ceiling:**
- Claude states plant heat equals site electrical power (2.5–8 MW) plus any solar-thermal input. It concludes a solar-thermal smelter could exceed 9 MWth, and that the 9 MWth ceiling holds only for all-electric routes.
- GPT states the 9 MWth case "needs justification against the 2.5–8 MWe site supply."
- These positions are not fully reconciled in the submissions.

**Area figures** are on different bases and are not directly comparable:
- Claude gives two-sided panel area at ε 0.85 with a 200 K sink. Its 9 MWth figures are about 14,000 m² at 300 K and about 730 m² at 600 K.
- GPT gives total emitting area at ε 0.9, with no sink or sunlight. Its figures are 2,400–21,800 m² at 300 K and 150–1,360 m² at 600 K. GPT labels these "optimistic screening values".

**What would settle it:** the route energy balance step on everyone's path, done to a single stated convention.

### D9. Coolant selection

- **Claude** proposes a band table:
  - 250–350 K: ammonia;
  - 350–500 K: water heat pipes or organic loop;
  - 500–800 K: NaK.
- **Gemini** proposes water or Dowtherm A at 350–500 K for the tug.
- **GPT** states that ammonia is not a generic coolant across 300–600 K and that "no coolant selection is established".

**What would settle it:** the coolant and materials selection testing in the early path steps.

## 4. Evidence register

### 4a. Cited by more than one model

| Evidence | Cited by | Notes and flags |
|---|---|---|
| ISS External ATCS pumped-ammonia loops and radiators | All three | Claude and Gemini: about 70 kWth at about 275 K. GPT: about 35 kW *published capacity* per loop, explicitly "not independently verified full-load calorimetry". GPT's source is the NASA Reference Guide to the ISS (2015); Claude and Gemini give none. |

### 4c. Strongest evidence for the rating

The strongest cited evidence is the ISS EATCS. It is the only item all three cite, two of the three give it a source, and all treat it as confident.

Even so, the models differ on what it represents:
- design capacity: about 70 kW (Claude);
- published rated capacity: 35 kW per loop (GPT);
- demonstrated rejection: GPT says full-load calorimetry is not established by the sources cited.

The ISS EVA-repair record (Claude, GPT) is the main evidence used *against* crediting autonomous long life.

All other heritage either comes from a single model or is marked unsure by at least one model.

**Points the panel must resolve before baselining the path:**
- the TRL 6 test scale (step 6; see D4);
- whether a flight element is required (step 7);
- whether the tug is qualified as a separate item (steps 8 and D1, D7);
- the service-life requirement (D6).

**GPT's qualification details**, offered as a checklist for steps 3–6:
- Dust: α/ε change against deposited mass.
- Leak isolation: demonstrated physical puncture, not command simulation only.
- Lifetime: endurance testing with a test-correlated degradation model.
- Gravity: relevant-gravity or flight testing where ground tests cannot bound two-phase or rotating behaviour.
- Scale: explicit validation of modular extrapolation.

**Fallbacks:**
- Claude: cap plant thermal power at what a demonstrated segment rejects within the mass budget, favouring ≥500 K rejection or direct hot-product radiation; then revert to 0A only.
- Gemini: drastically reduce throughput, or revert to 0A only.
- GPT: select independently qualified stationary processing and lower-power modular tugs if demand and economics close; otherwise 0A only.
